summary:
We built a harmonized burning-activity calendar for Spain (November 2000 to December 2025) that combines MODIS (Terra and Aqua) and VIIRS (Suomi NPP and NOAA-20) active-fire detections into one consistent time series. The data is cleaned, filtered by confidence, and assigned to provinces. Non-vegetation heat sources, such as the 2021 La Palma volcanic eruption and industrial sites, are flagged and excluded. Detections are converted to unique 1 km burning square-days, VIIRS is filtered by fire radiative power, and both sensors are scaled to match Aqua. Validated on the overlap years, the conversions have a typical yearly error of about 7 to 9%, so changes in the series reflect fire activity and not the satellite.

The web app lets users select a province or click the map, choose a date range, and explore monthly and daily calendar heatmaps, harmonized versus raw sensor series, and any year compared with the historical average. Users can download harmonized daily counts and individual hotspot detections as CSV files.

It gives emergency managers a reliable fire history: when fires peak, which years stood out, and how current activity compares. The method can be reused for other regions.
details:
We harmonized NASA FIRMS active-fire detections from MODIS (Terra and Aqua) and VIIRS (Suomi NPP and NOAA-20) into one consistent burning-activity series for Spain, from November 2000 to December 2025.

The pipeline has four stages. First, we cleaned the data: we removed duplicates and invalid values, filtered low-confidence detections with a separate rule for each sensor, kept only presumed vegetation fires, and assigned every detection to one of Spain’s 52 provinces. Second, we flagged non-vegetation heat sources instead of deleting them: the 2021-22 La Palma volcanic eruption, which produced about 30,000 detections, and 3,908 detections from static industrial sites that appeared in the same 1 km square in 15 or more different years. Third, we put the sensors on a common footing. We count unique 1 km squares with a detection per day instead of raw points, because VIIRS’s finer pixels produce about 1.8 points per square-day against 1.1 for MODIS. VIIRS is then limited to detections with fire radiative power of 6 MW or more, and the counts of each sensor are scaled to match Aqua (VIIRS by about 0.72, Terra by about 0.915). Fourth, we built a single series: Terra-based until mid-2002, Aqua until 2011, and VIIRS from 2012, with a source label on every row.

The Streamlit web app reads this harmonized dataset. Users select a province (from a dropdown or by clicking the map) and a date range. They get a monthly calendar heatmap and a daily calendar for a single year, a chart comparing the harmonized series with the raw Terra, Aqua and VIIRS series, a comparison of any year against the historical average, and a map of individual detections. Both the harmonized daily counts and the individual hotspot detections can be downloaded as CSV files for the selection.

Benefits and intended impact

Without harmonization, the arrival of VIIRS in 2012 looks like a change in fire activity when it is really a change in sensor. Our series lets emergency managers and researchers read patterns, trends and anomalies without worrying about the sensor of origin: which months are the fire season, which years stood out, and how a current fire compares with the past. The method is not tied to Spain, so it can be run on other regions.

Tools

Python, pandas, NumPy, GeoPandas and Parquet (pyarrow) for processing; Google Colab and Google Drive for the shared notebooks and data; NASA FIRMS (archive download and API) as the data source; Natural Earth for province boundaries; Streamlit for the web app.

What is creative

  • Instead of choosing a conversion method in advance, we tested several and kept the one the data supported. A single ratio failed (the VIIRS-to-Aqua ratio was 3.9 and varied from 2.7 to 6.0 across months). A fitted curve and a seasonal fit both underestimated or overestimated the extreme years. Filtering VIIRS by fire radiative power stabilized the relationship and brought the yearly error down to about 7%.
  • Flagging instead of deleting means users can see how much the volcano and industrial sites affect the results.
  • The app can show the raw sensor series beside the harmonized one, so users can see the harmonization working.

Factors we considered

We validated each conversion by hiding one year at a time and predicting it. The typical yearly error was about 7% for VIIRS to Aqua and about 9% for Terra to Aqua. We also identified limitations and are stating them in the project:

  • The counts are burning square-days, not raw hotspots, and the app explains the difference to users.
  • The FRP cut-off was tuned on the overlap years, so the validation is slightly optimistic.
  • The Terra scaling is assumed to hold for 2000 to 2002, when Aqua did not yet exist.
  • Satellite orbits have drifted over the years.
  • Daily counts are noisier than monthly ones.
  • 2000 and 2002 are partial years.
  • The data currently ends in December 2025.
